guide_line: Use the mole ratio and the molar mass to convert between grams and moles of reactants and products.
steps: Balance the equation. The coefficients are the mole ratio.
Change a given mass into moles by dividing by the molar mass. Change a solution volume into moles with molarity times liters.
Multiply by the mole ratio: moles wanted = moles given times (coefficient wanted / coefficient given).
If the question asks for grams, multiply the moles you want by that substance's molar mass.

Use these OpenStax atomic masses at full precision: H 1.008, C 12.011, N 14.007, O 15.999, Na 22.990, Mg 24.305, Al 26.982, S 32.06, Cl 35.45, Ca 40.078, Fe 55.845, Ag 107.868. Round only the final answer, to 4 significant figures.

worked_example.q: How many grams of H2O form when 4.000 g of H2 burns in excess O2? The equation is 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O.
steps: Molar mass of H2 = 2(1.008) = 2.016 g/mol. Moles of H2 = 4.000 / 2.016 = 1.984 mol.
The ratio is 2 mol H2O / 2 mol H2, so moles of water = 1.984 mol.
Molar mass of H2O = 2(1.008) + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol. Mass = 1.984 mol times 18.015 g/mol = 35.74 g.

similar_problem.q: How many grams of H2O form when 8.000 g of H2 burns in excess O2? The equation is 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O.
similar_problem.hint: Use the same two molar masses as the example. The new starting mass of H2 is 8.000 g.

problems.q: How many grams of H2O form when 4.000 g of H2 burns in excess O2? 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O. Include the unit g.
problems.why: Moles of H2 = 4.000 / 2.016 = 1.984 mol. The ratio to water is 1 to 1. Mass of H2O = 1.984 mol times 18.015 g/mol = 35.74 g.
hints: Divide 4.000 g by the molar mass of H2, 2.016 g/mol, then multiply by 18.015 g/mol of water.

problems.q: How many grams of H2O form when 8.000 g of H2 burns in excess O2? 2 H2 + O2 -> 2 H2O. Include the unit g.
problems.why: Moles of H2 = 8.000 / 2.016 = 3.968 mol. The ratio to water is 1 to 1. Mass of H2O = 3.968 mol times 18.015 g/mol = 71.49 g.
hints: 8.000 g of H2 divided by 2.016 g/mol gives the moles, and the water ratio is 1 to 1.

problems.q: How many moles of O2 react with 0.2500 mol of C3H8? C3H8 + 5 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. Include the unit mol.
problems.why: The ratio is 5 mol O2 / 1 mol C3H8. Moles of O2 = 0.2500 times 5 = 1.250 mol.
hints: The coefficient ratio is 5 mol O2 per 1 mol C3H8, and you start with 0.2500 mol of propane.

problems.q: How many grams of CO2 form from 0.4500 mol of C3H8 burned in excess O2? C3H8 + 5 O2 -> 3 CO2 + 4 H2O. Include the unit g.
problems.why: Moles of CO2 = 0.4500 times 3 = 1.350 mol. Molar mass of CO2 = 12.011 + 2(15.999) = 44.009 g/mol. Mass = 1.350 times 44.009 = 59.41 g.
hints: 0.4500 mol of propane makes 1.350 mol of CO2, and CO2 is 12.011 + 2(15.999) g/mol.

problems.q: How many grams of NaCl form when 5.000 g of Na reacts with excess Cl2? 2 Na + Cl2 -> 2 NaCl. Include the unit g.
problems.why: Moles of Na = 5.000 / 22.990 = 0.2175 mol. The ratio to NaCl is 1 to 1. Molar mass of NaCl = 22.990 + 35.45 = 58.440 g/mol. Mass = 0.2175 times 58.440 = 12.71 g.
hints: 5.000 g divided by 22.990 g/mol is the moles of Na. NaCl is 22.990 + 35.45 g/mol and the ratio is 1 to 1.

problems.q: 40.00 mL of 0.1250 M AgNO3 reacts with excess NaCl. How many moles of AgCl form? Include the unit mol.
problems.why: Moles of AgNO3 = 0.04000 L times 0.1250 mol/L = 0.005000 mol. The silver ratio is 1 to 1, so AgCl is 0.005000 mol.
hints: Change 40.00 mL into 0.04000 L, multiply by 0.1250 mol/L, and keep the 1-to-1 silver ratio.

problems.q: 40.00 mL of 0.1250 M AgNO3 reacts with excess NaCl. How many grams of AgCl form? Include the unit g.
problems.why: Moles of AgCl = 0.04000 times 0.1250 = 0.005000 mol. Molar mass of AgCl = 107.868 + 35.45 = 143.318 g/mol. Mass = 0.005000 times 143.318 = 0.7166 g.
hints: You need 0.005000 mol of AgCl. Its molar mass is 107.868 + 35.45.

problems.q: How many grams of Al are needed to produce 25.00 g of Al2O3? 4 Al + 3 O2 -> 2 Al2O3. Include the unit g.
hints: Al2O3 is 2(26.982) + 3(15.999) g/mol, and the metal ratio is 4 mol Al for 2 mol oxide.

problems.q: What volume, in mL, of 0.2500 M HCl reacts with 1.250 g of Ca(OH)2? Ca(OH)2 + 2 HCl -> CaCl2 + 2 H2O. Include the unit mL.
hints: Ca(OH)2 is 40.078 + 2(15.999) + 2(1.008) g/mol, it takes 2 HCl, and the acid is 0.2500 M.

problems.q: Heating CaCO3 makes CaO and CO2. How many grams of CO2 form from 12.50 g of CaCO3? Include the unit g.
problems.why: Molar mass of CaCO3 = 40.078 + 12.011 + 3(15.999) = 100.086 g/mol. Moles = 12.50 / 100.086 = 0.1249 mol. The ratio to CO2 is 1 to 1. Mass of CO2 = 0.1249 times 44.009 = 5.496 g.
hints: CaCO3 is 40.078 + 12.011 + 3(15.999) g/mol. One mole of it makes one mole of CO2 at 44.009 g/mol.

problems.q: How many grams of Fe form when 8.400 g of Fe2O3 reacts with excess CO? Fe2O3 + 3 CO -> 2 Fe + 3 CO2. Include the unit g.
problems.why: Molar mass of Fe2O3 = 2(55.845) + 3(15.999) = 159.687 g/mol. Moles of oxide = 8.400 / 159.687 = 0.05260 mol. Moles of Fe = 0.1052 mol. Mass of Fe = 0.1052 times 55.845 = 5.875 g.
hints: Fe2O3 is 2(55.845) + 3(15.999) g/mol. The ratio is 2 mol Fe per 1 mol of the oxide.

problems.q: How many moles of H2 form when 0.03600 mol of Zn reacts with excess HCl? Zn + 2 HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Include the unit mol.
problems.why: The coefficient ratio is 1 mol H2 / 1 mol Zn. Moles of H2 = 0.03600 mol.
hints: The balanced equation shows one H2 for each Zn, so 0.03600 mol of zinc makes 0.03600 mol of gas.

problems.q: How many grams of O2 are needed to burn 6.000 g of Mg? 2 Mg + O2 -> 2 MgO. Include the unit g.
problems.why: Moles of Mg = 6.000 / 24.305 = 0.2469 mol. Moles of O2 = half of that = 0.1234 mol. Mass of O2 = 0.1234 times 31.998 = 3.950 g.
hints: Divide 6.000 g by 24.305 g/mol of Mg, take half of those moles because 2 Mg need 1 O2, then use 31.998 g/mol.
